promise: After this you can explain what a rate limit and a 429 response are, how a limiter counts with windows and buckets, and why a shared count is the hard part.

terms.definition: One message from a program to a server asking it to do something, such as send a web page.
Whatever sends requests: a browser, an app, a script, or another server.
A three-digit number in a web server's reply that says how the request went, such as 404 for not found.

before.note: You do not need Caching or Consistent Hashing for the stages below. They matter on the topic page, where the posts spread counters over many cache servers. If the three terms are familiar, you are ready.

stages.name: Basics
body: A server can only answer so many requests. A rate limit is a rule that caps how many requests one client may make in a period of time. When a client goes over, the server turns the extra requests away instead of doing the work for them.

HTTP has a status code for this: 429 Too Many Requests. The standard describes it as the client having sent too many requests in a given amount of time, which is what rate limiting means [[rfc6585]]. It leaves the server free to decide what counts as one client, for example by the credentials or cookie a request carries, and over what scope to count [[rfc6585]].

Many limiters describe a limit with two numbers: a steady rate and a burst. AWS explains its API Gateway this way, as a token bucket: a token counts for a request, the rate is how fast tokens are added to the bucket, and the burst is the size of the bucket [[aws-apigw-throttling]]. That is how AWS's service behaves. Other systems count in other ways, and the next stages look at some of them.

terms.definition: A cap on how many requests a client may make in a period of time.
The HTTP status code a server can send when a client has sent too many requests in a given time.
In AWS's description: a bucket that receives tokens at a steady rate, where each request takes one token.
In AWS's description of its token bucket, the size of the bucket: how many requests can pass at once.

reading.what: What the status code means, and that the server may add a hint about when to try again.

stages.name: How it works
body: Whatever the design, a limiter does three things for each request: it finds the key the request belongs to, updates the count kept for that key, and compares the count with the limit. If the count is within the limit the request goes on, and if not it is turned away.

NGINX's limit_req module shows one way to count. It limits the rate of requests per key, for example per client IP address, using what it calls the leaky bucket method [[nginx-limit-req]]. You define a shared memory zone with the key and the rate, then switch it on for a location. In the docs' example, requests are held to an average of one per second, with bursts of up to five [[nginx-limit-req]]. Requests over the rate are delayed so they are processed at the rate, until their number passes the burst size, and then they are rejected. The default status for a rejected request is 503, and it can be changed [[nginx-limit-req]].

Redis shows another way, with a counter. Its INCR page builds a rate limiter that keeps one counter for every IP address for every different second, adds one to it with each request, and sets it to expire so old counters clean themselves up. The page's example allows up to ten requests per second for each IP address [[redis-incr]]. Counting in separate slices of time like this is a fixed window. The page also shows a second, single-counter variant and warns that it has a race condition that can leave a counter without an expiry, and shows a way to fix it [[redis-incr]].

A third way to count, the sliding window, is not explained in the official sources used on this page. The [Cloudflare post](/topic/rate-limiting#cloudflare-rate-limiting-2017) on the topic page walks through it with numbers.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: A limiter on one machine only sees that machine's traffic. Envoy's documentation separates two kinds. A local rate limit is applied inside each Envoy instance and needs no outside service. A global rate limit coordinates across many Envoy instances through an external service [[envoy-global-rl]].

For global limits, Envoy calls a gRPC rate limit service on each new connection or each HTTP request, passing a domain and a set of descriptors that say what is being counted. The page names a reference implementation written in Go that uses Redis as its backend [[envoy-global-rl]]. It describes global limiting as a fit when many downstream hosts send traffic to a few upstream hosts, where circuit breaking alone is hard to tune [[envoy-global-rl]].

The two can be combined. The page says a local token bucket can absorb very large bursts of load that might otherwise overwhelm the global service, and the global limit then gives finer control [[envoy-global-rl]]. NGINX also has a way to try a limit safely: in dry run mode the limit is not enforced, but excess requests are still counted in the shared memory zone [[nginx-limit-req]]. Its burst settings go further than a plain cap, with a delay setting that decides at which point excess requests start to be delayed and a nodelay setting that stops delaying them within the burst [[nginx-limit-req]].
On the topic page, the Cloudflare and Databricks posts show two other answers to the same problem: where a shared count lives, and how to keep it off the path of every request.

terms.definition: A limit applied inside each proxy instance on its own, with no outside service.
A limit shared across many proxy instances by asking an external rate limit service.
In Envoy's global limiting, the details sent to the rate limit service that say what a request should be counted under.
In NGINX, a mode where the limit is not enforced but excess requests are still counted.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: A limit is a target more than a wall. AWS says that its throttles and quotas are applied on a best-effort basis and should be treated as targets, not guaranteed ceilings [[aws-apigw-throttling]]. That is a statement about AWS's service. It is a useful warning for any design where counts are shared or reported with a delay, because the real traffic can overshoot the limit a little.

A rejected client should be told what to do next. The 429 standard says a response may include a Retry-After header saying how long to wait [[rfc6585]]. The HTTP specification defines that header as either a date or a number of seconds, and describes it with 503 responses and redirects [[rfc9110]]. AWS says that when clients are throttled with a 429, they can resubmit the failed requests in a way that respects the limit, [[aws-apigw-throttling]]. In our own words, that means retrying more slowly.

There is also work to tell clients about their quota before they hit it. An Internet-Draft from the IETF's HTTPAPI working group proposes two header fields: one that describes a server's quota policies, and one that conveys the quota currently available [[ietf-ratelimit-draft]]. It is a draft, a work in progress and not a standard. The header names and meaning may change, so do not build on them as if they were settled.

The trade-off underneath it all is accuracy against cost. A more exact shared count costs more time on every request, which is why the posts on the topic page accept approximate counts in return for keeping counting off the request path.

terms.definition: An HTTP header that tells a client how long to wait before trying again, as a date or a number of seconds.
A limit that is aimed for but not guaranteed. AWS describes its throttles and quotas this way.
Two header fields proposed in an IETF Internet-Draft to describe a server's quota policies and the quota currently available. A draft, not a standard.
Traffic that gets over the limit before it is stopped.

misconceptions.myth: A 429 response means the server is broken.
misconceptions.truth: It means the client sent too many requests in a given time, and the server may add a Retry-After header to say when to try again [[rfc6585]].

misconceptions.myth: Every rate limiter works like a token bucket.
misconceptions.truth: NGINX's limit_req module uses the leaky bucket method [[nginx-limit-req]], the Redis page counts requests per second with a counter [[redis-incr]], and AWS API Gateway uses a token bucket [[aws-apigw-throttling]].

misconceptions.myth: A rate limit is an exact ceiling.
misconceptions.truth: AWS says its throttles and quotas are best-effort targets, not guaranteed ceilings [[aws-apigw-throttling]]. That is AWS's behavior, and other systems differ, but any shared count can overshoot a little.
